title: The development of creative imagination and symbolic thinking through thematic social role-play activity.
abstract: Grounded in Vygotsky's cultural-historical paradigm, this article presents a theoretical analysis of the role of thematic social role-play in preschool psychological development, positioning it not merely as a recreational activity but as the leading activity driving psychological maturation. Within this framework, we examine how high-level play serves as the critical foundation for the genesis of creative imagination and symbolic thought-all essential components of the developing child's psychological neoformations. Specifically, we analyze the trajectory of adult-guided orientation, illustrating its necessity in transforming initial, fragmented play behaviors into advanced, mature role-play characterized by reflective initiative, internal rules, and symbolic verbal actions. Furthermore, we delineate the transition from object-substituted actions to deep psychological internalization. Based on this theoretical synthesis, we hypothesize that a child's readiness for formal school learning is a direct function of the semiotic and structural complexity of their thematic social role-play. We propose that the more intentional, collaborative, and creative the play behavior, the stronger the cognitive, volitional, and social foundations for subsequent academic success. Finally, we argue for an educational shift that prioritizes structured, high-level thematic social role-play not as a leisure choice, but as a core, non-negotiable developmental necessity in early childhood education.
